nameStory: Canada wild lettuce gets its name from its northern range and its resemblance to garden lettuce, sharing the same genus Lactuca. Like its cultivated cousin, this wild plant produces a milky white sap when broken, which is where the name 'lettuce' originally comes from - 'lac' meaning milk in Latin.
description: Canada wild lettuce is a tall, slender biennial plant that can tower up to 6 feet high, making it one of the giants of New England's wildflower world. It belongs to the daisy family and produces clusters of small, pale yellow flowers at the top of its stem. The plant has deeply lobed leaves that give it a somewhat lettuce-like appearance, though it's much taller and more dramatic than any salad green you've ever seen.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pale yellow flower heads about half an inch wide, arranged in loose clusters at the top of the plant. Each flower head has only ray petals (like daisy petals) with no central disc - they look like tiny dandelion flowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves that feel smooth to the touch, sometimes with small teeth along the edges. Break a leaf and you'll see milky white sap ooze out - this is the most reliable identification feature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Impressively tall plant, often 4-6 feet high, growing straight up from a single thick taproot. The overall shape is like a narrow tower with flowers clustered at the very top

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Dark-colored seeds about a quarter-inch long, each topped with fluffy white bristles (called pappus) that help them float on the wind like dandelion seeds

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy stem that also bleeds milky white sap when cut or broken - you can test this by carefully scratching the stem with your fingernail

habitat: Look for Canada wild lettuce in disturbed soils, field edges, roadsides, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in sunny to partially shaded locations with rich, moist soil, often appearing in areas that have been cleared or disturbed. You'll commonly find it growing alongside other tall weeds and wildflowers in abandoned lots, along fence rows, and at the margins of agricultural areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as rosettes of lobed leaves close to the ground. First-year plants spend the season building up energy in their taproot and won't flower.
seasonality.summer: Second-year plants shoot up dramatically and bloom from mid to late summer, producing their characteristic pale yellow flower clusters. This is prime identification time when the milky sap is most obvious.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and produce fluffy white seed heads that disperse on autumn breezes. The tall dried stalks often persist, looking like brown skeletons in the landscape.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may remain standing through winter as dry, brittle stalks. Underground, the taproots of first-year plants survive the cold, ready to send up flowering stalks the following year.

funFact: Despite being called 'wild lettuce,' this plant contains compounds that can be mildly toxic and bitter - it's definitely not meant for your salad bowl! Indigenous peoples traditionally used the milky sap medicinally, but modern foragers should admire this towering beauty from a distance.
confusionNotes: Canada wild lettuce can be confused with other tall wild lettuces, but the milky white sap is the dead giveaway for the entire lettuce family. Remember: 'When in doubt, check for white sap spout!' If it doesn't bleed white when broken, it's not a wild lettuce.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while it's called 'lettuce' and is related to garden lettuce, Canada wild lettuce is not edible and can actually cause stomach upset. The 'wild lettuce' name refers purely to the botanical relationship and the milky sap they share, not to any culinary use.
compareHints: Canada wild lettuce differs from tall blue lettuce by its pale yellow flowers (versus blue), and from prickly lettuce by its smooth leaves without spines. Unlike hairy lettuce, Canada wild lettuce has smooth, hairless leaves and stems, making it feel pleasant to touch rather than rough or bristly.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the wild lettuces, tall blue lettuce stands out for its exceptional height and pale blue flowers - Canada wild lettuce has yellow blooms, while prickly lettuce has spiny leaves and is much shorter.
Prickly lettuce stands out from other wild lettuces by its prickly leaf undersides and the tendency for leaves to twist vertically.

Among New England's wild lettuces, hairy lettuce is the fuzziest—literally! While tall blue lettuce is smooth-leaved and prickly lettuce has actual spines, hairy lettuce feels soft and downy to the touch.
Garden lettuce differs from its wild Lactuca relatives by having much broader, more tender leaves without the deeply cut or prickly edges found on species like prickly lettuce or Canada wild lettuce.
